summary: Redwood AE+SE ran a focused demo for Vertex Retail showing multi-tenant long-context handling, high TPS behavior, streaming backpressure modes, and how the console/Optimize suggests configs. Customer raised concerns about cold-start latencies, KV cache eviction under tenant isolation, and circuit breaker timeouts. Agreed next steps: share perf spreadsheet, run controlled benchmark, and prepare pilot with dedicated pool and KV cache enabled.
topics: KV cache eviction and multi-tenant isolation
transcript:
Header:
Date: 2026-03-12
Start: 16:00 UTC
Duration: 57 minutes
Attendees: Maya Patel (Redwood AE), Ethan Brooks (Redwood SE), Lina Gomez (Vertex ML Platform), Arjun Rao (Vertex Infra), Sofia Kim (Vertex Head of Data)

[00:00] Maya Patel: Hi everyone, thanks for joining. I'm Maya, AE at Redwood. Ethan will walk through a targeted demo showing long context + high throughput behavior plus how our console shows backpressure.
[00:18] Lina Gomez: Hi! Excited. Quick note, we're particularly worried about multi-tenant eviction and cold starts, and also streaming timeouts in our chat UI.
[00:29] Ethan Brooks: Great, we built a scenari - scenario that mimics a retail recommendation session — multiple tenants, each with long conversation histories, some sessions 30-50k tokens, and bursts up to ~2k rps. We'll step through p50/p95 latency and then show the circuit behavior when backpressure happens.
[00:48] Arjun Rao: Can you clarify dedicated vs hosted here? We need data isolation but not sure we want full private yet.
[00:57] Maya Patel: Yep, we'll call out differences. Dedicated gives you reserved GPU pools and tenant isolation at infra level; hosted can be routed with tenancy policy but less isolated, though we offer VPC peering options for hosted as well.
[01:10] Ethan Brooks: Kicking off the demo — first, live API call stream to a long-session model. Note the session includes KV cache hits for prefix tokens to keep decode costs down.
[01:29] [01:29] Speaker 1 (automatic): Um, yeah, okay, we see token streaming now, partials coming...
[01:36] Ethan Brooks: You'll notice the token rate is steady. Now I trigger a simulated tenant burst that hits ~1800 rps across 4 model shards. Watch the console metrics: queue length, batch size, and tail latency.
[01:55] [02:02] Lina Gomez: I already see queue jumping to 120ms then 800ms — is that expected?
[02:09] Ethan Brooks: So what you're seeing is short-lived backpressure. Our runtime will widen batching to improve throughput; that increases per-request latency but reduces per-token cost. The console has an SLO slider to balance latency vs cost.
[02:28] Arjun Rao: What about streaming timeouts? Our frontend cancels at 2s and retries; will that cause repeated cold starts?
[02:36] Ethan Brooks: Good question. We instrumented a few defenses: automatic semantic retry suppression, session-affinity routing to keep KV cached workers warm, and an application-level circuit breaker. If the client cancels early repeatedly, the runtime can detect and apply a soft-throttle to that source to avoid thrashing.
[02:52] Sofia Kim: Can you show the KV eviction behavior? We have concerns about one tenant evicting another's keys on shared nodes.
[03:01] Ethan Brooks: Sure — in hosted multi-tenant the KV cache is logically isolated per tenant but physically shared; eviction is per-tenant LRU, so tenant A cannot evict tenant B's entries. If you need hard isolation, Dedicated with tenant pinning gives physical separation.
[03:19] Lina Gomez: When you say LRU per-tenant, if tenant has lots of long sessions, could their entries grow and cause overall node memory pressure?
[03:28] Ethan Brooks: Yes, that's why we have per-tenant cache quotas and eviction policies and we also expose those metrics to the Console Optimize tab so you can tune quotas or adopt aggressive prefix truncation.
[03:42] [03:45] Speaker 2: (mumbles) okay that's helpful
[03:48] Ethan Brooks: Now I'm going to flip to the Optimize recommendations — for this workload we suggest: prefetch top-10 tokens, enable dynamic batching with max batch 64 for 8k contexts, and use int8 quant profile for the 70% of traffic that's low-latency tolerant.
[04:06] Lina Gomez: Wait, int8 — are you seeing any quality regressions?
[04:13] Ethan Brooks: Small regression in some reranking tasks; we recommend A/Bing with an eval set. Optimize surfaces model-level tradeoffs and can auto-rollout to a small % with canary.
[04:24] Arjun Rao: What about timeouts at the network level — we have 10s egress windows with our cloud vendor, and if Redwood takes longer we get errors.
[04:34] Maya Patel: We allow you to set per-route timeouts and have graceful fallback policies — e.g., reduce context to last 2k tokens, fallback to a smaller model, or return partial streaming with a 'continued' token.
[04:47] Ethan Brooks: Let's simulate an extreme: drop one model shard and saturate others. You'll see the circuit breaker icon go orange. The system will then reroute low-priority traffic to a cheaper model to preserve SLOs.
[05:02] [05:09] Lina Gomez: How deterministic is reroute? We need to ensure critical billing operations always get high-quality responses.
[05:16] Ethan Brooks: You can tag routes with priority and apply guaranteed reserved slots on Dedicated pools. For hosted, you can configure fallback hierarchies by route. We also support token-level billing offsets to prefer high-priority traffic.
[05:33] Arjun Rao: For the benchmark run — do you require a VPC peering or can we run from our infra?
[05:40] Maya Patel: For initial tests you can run from your infra hitting hosted endpoints; for isolation and latency-accurate numbers, Dedicated in the same region is best. If you want us to bootstrap a private pilot we can provide an on-prem option but that takes longer.
[05:52] Ethan Brooks: Okay I'm switching to a stress script that opens many streaming connections and sometimes cancels mid-stream to mimic flaky mobile clients. Watch how the runtime records 'cancellations' and 'incomplete decodes' in telemetry.
[06:08] [06:15] Speaker 3: there's a slight stutter on the stream, partial tokens arrive then a gap
[06:19] Ethan Brooks: That's the batching expansion coming in — it deliberately holds for a few ms to fill batch. In the Console trace you can see 'batching hold' events with metrics for hold_time and final_batch_size.
[06:32] Lina Gomez: Can we set a hard limit to avoid any holding for our chat UX? We prefer lots of smaller responses over occasional stalls.
[06:40] Ethan Brooks: Yes, set the batching policy to aggressive low-latency: max_hold_ms = 3, max_batch_size = 8, and enable prefix-KV prewarm. That reduces throughput efficiency but keeps tail latency low. Optimize can recommend exact values per workload.
[06:54] Arjun Rao: In that mode what's the expected cost delta?
[06:58] Ethan Brooks: Rough numbers: low-latency batching can increase per-token cost by ~40% vs throughput-optimized. But with KV caching and prefix truncation you can recover some of that. We'll put exact modeled numbers in the perf spreadsheet.
[07:12] [07:15] Maya Patel: Quick pause — any security blockers here? Lina?
[07:20] Lina Gomez: SSO, KMS ops, audit logs — we need RBAC integration and HSM-backed keys. Also, data residency for EU customers.
[07:29] Maya Patel: Redwood Private supports customer-managed KMS and HSM, detailed audit logs, and you can pin a region for hosted. We'll send the security pack.
[07:38] Sofia Kim: Also curious about cost modeling — we have fluctuating seasonality; can Redwood smooth costs?
[07:45] Ethan Brooks: You can combine reserved capacity commitments with autoscaling burst for seasonality. Optimize provides cost forecasts based on real traffic traces.
[07:56] [08:01] Speaker 1: (faint) okay wow that's useful
[08:04] Ethan Brooks: Now we'll induce sustained high TPS for 2 minutes. Notice early on latency P95 jumps then stabilizes as batching achieves higher utilization.
[08:20] [08:25] Lina Gomez: I'm watching 95th -> 1.2s then down to 600ms after ~20s. So there's an initial ramp. Can we reduce that ramp?
[08:33] Ethan Brooks: You can keep a small warm pool of pinned workers per tenant, and we also provide a prewarm API to load KV in advance. That eliminates much of the ramp at some cost.
[08:43] Arjun Rao: If we enable prewarm, do we pay for idle GPU cycles?
[08:47] Ethan Brooks: On Dedicated it's just reserved capacity; on hosted it's burst + warm-worker charges. We'll show the breakdown in the cost tab.
[08:57] Maya Patel: I'll share a sample cost calc with both reserve vs burst toggles.
[09:02] [09:08] Ethan Brooks: Now I'm toggling simulated network slow path to force streaming timeouts at the client side — see the console logging repeated cancels. Watch the circuit engage: after N cancels in window, requests are queued under a 'soft-throttle' label and we return structured error with suggested client backoff.
[09:27] Lina Gomez: How aggressive is that? We don't want our users to see too many errors, just slightly degraded responses.
[09:33] Ethan Brooks: The default is conservative; it marks low-priority routes for fallback rather than hard reject. You can tune the thresholds per route.
[09:40] Sofia Kim: Is there a way to see which tenant caused the throttle? For auditing we need a replayable timeline.
[09:46] Ethan Brooks: Yes, audit logs include request_id -> tenant_id mapping, and the Console trace has an exportable CSV with timeline and event codes.
[09:55] [10:00] Speaker 2: (typing) good
[10:03] Ethan Brooks: Next, model fallback demo: I trigger failure on main model; the runtime switches to smaller model and continues streaming partial responses with a 'quality' score attached. Note how the Optimize console warns about mismatch and flags certain prompts where quality drops below threshold.
[10:22] Lina Gomez: That 'quality' score — is it internal eval or can we supply our own eval set?
[10:28] Ethan Brooks: You can supply your own eval set; Optimize will run automatic regression checks and can block rollouts if regressions exceed your configured tolerance.
[10:35] Arjun Rao: For our pilot we'll want to run a 30-minute benchmark that mimics holiday peak: long histories, 3k rps bursts, many cancels. What do you need from us?
[10:44] Maya Patel: Sample prompts, traffic distribution, and a small set of ground-truth checks. We'll prepare the harness and share instructions.
[10:51] [11:00] Ethan Brooks: Switching to Console: here you can see per-route SLOs, token-level cost, and a heatmap of KV hit rates. I click into a tenant and show memory-per-tenant and eviction events.
[11:15] Lina Gomez: Hmm the eviction graph spikes; can you annotate which traffic pattern caused that?
[11:20] Ethan Brooks: Yup — this spike correlates with tenanted bulk imports; Optimize suggests trimming historical prefixes for these imports and enabling per-tenant cache quotas.
[11:32] Arjun Rao: Does Redwood support prioritizing system-critical requests at kernel level? e.g., payments webhooks?
[11:39] Ethan Brooks: Yes — route priority tags map to scheduling priority. For Dedicated we can reserve slots; for hosted we use token-priority and preemption policies.
[11:49] [11:52] Speaker 3: um, what about read-after-write consistency for KV? If we write a recall token, will subsequent reads immediately see it?
[11:59] Ethan Brooks: KV is eventually consistent within a single request boundary but we provide strong-affinity options when you use dedicated sessions with pinned workers. For strict consistency patterns we recommend Dedicated with session pinning.
[12:12] Lina Gomez: Can you demo a canary rollback? We want to see how fast a bad model can be reverted.
[12:18] Ethan Brooks: Sure. I roll out a canary of 10% to the model family, we'll show the anomaly detection kicking in and then automatic rollback.
[12:30] [12:35] Maya Patel: Also note you can tie canary to KPIs: latency, perplexity, or your custom eval metric.
[12:41] Lina Gomez: One more question — tenant billing attribution. If a tenant causes thrash that increases shared cost, how is it attributed?
[12:50] Maya Patel: We attribute by request_id and can optionally bill by token or by effective cost share. For multi-tenant hosted customers we provide an apportioned view; for Dedicated it's straightforward per-tenant capacity mapping.
[13:03] [13:10] Ethan Brooks: Okay, I'll induce a node failure to show graceful degradation — watch how inflight sessions continue on fallback workers and new sessions get queued with a fallback policy.
[13:24] Lina Gomez: I see some partials cut — is there a guarantee for no data loss?
[13:30] Ethan Brooks: In-flight streaming can produce partials; we guarantee request-level idempotency if you reissue with the same request_id, and the Console shows 'continued' tokens to stitch responses.
[13:41] Arjun Rao: For mobile UX we prefer retries — how do you recommend client backoff?
[13:46] Ethan Brooks: Exponential backoff with jitter, combined with client-side session affinity cookie. Avoid immediate cancel/retry loops — Redwood will adopt a soft-throttle if it detects that pattern.
[13:58] [14:04] Speaker 1: (background noise) okay
[14:07] Ethan Brooks: Quick demo of Optimize cost-suggester: upload a traffic sample and it outputs quantization, batching, and split-routing suggestions. For this dataset it recommends shifting 60% of search traffic to int8 small model and keep 40% on main model for HQ tasks.
[14:23] Lina Gomez: We need to validate quality before we shift. Does Optimize support canary with traffic mirroring?
[14:30] Ethan Brooks: Yes, traffic mirror to a shadow model for full-fidelity quality checks without affecting users.
[14:36] Sofia Kim: What telemetry do we get in the pilot? We need raw traces for offline analysis.
[14:42] Maya Patel: You get per-token timing traces, request-level metadata, KV hit/miss logs, and exported CSVs. For Private deployments we can also give raw logs to your SIEM via S3/secure transport.
[14:55] [15:00] Ethan Brooks: Time check — about halfway through. Any burning topics we missed?
[15:06] Lina Gomez: Can you show how to tune the SLO slider for our use case? We want 95th under 800ms for checkout but can accept 2s for recommendations.
[15:16] Ethan Brooks: Sure — in Console you define route-level SLOs and assign fallback policies. I'll set up a sample: route /checkout p95 target 800ms with fallback to preferred model variant and reserved slots.
[15:31] [15:40] Speaker 2: (agreeing) nice
[15:42] Ethan Brooks: Now a quick deep-dive into backpressure metrics: we log hold_time_ms, batch_size, queue_depth, and cancellation_rate. We have alerting hooks for queue_depth > threshold and cancellation_rate spike.
[15:58] Lina Gomez: Alerts to Slack/PagerDuty — good. Do they include request context for debugging?
[16:04] Ethan Brooks: Yes, they include trace_id and tenant_id and link to Console trace.
[16:12] Arjun Rao: A practical question — what's the onboarding time for Dedicated? We may want a two-week pilot with Dedicated capacity.
[16:19] Maya Patel: Dedicated typically 2-4 weeks for basic setup; 4-8 for advanced private/on-prem. For pilot we can fast-track a small reserved pool in 2 weeks.
[16:29] Lina Gomez: Ok that's reasonable.
[16:33] [16:35] Ethan Brooks: Last demo — simulate client timeout loops: repeated cancel/retry. Console shows elevated cancellation_rate and the runtime applies token-based damping. I switch on 'soft-throttle' policy which injects Retry-After; client reduces retry rate and system stabilizes.
[16:55] Sofia Kim: Do we get the ability to inspect which routes got throttled?
[17:00] Ethan Brooks: Yep — rates per route/tenant in Console with download.
[17:05] Lina Gomez: This all looks promising. A few notes for action items: we'll share traffic trace; we want the perf spreadsheet and security docs; and we want a concrete cost estimate for a 2-week dedicated pilot.
[17:19] Maya Patel: Absolutely — I'll send those items. Any other Qs?
[17:23] [17:28] Speaker 1: no, thank you
[17:30] Maya Patel: Thanks everyone, we'll follow up with the email and calendar invites.
[17:36] [17:40] Ethan Brooks: One last tip — when you run the benchmark, include a mix of long-session reads and short stateless calls; that'll show the real mixing cost.
[17:51] Lina Gomez: noted, thanks.
[17:55] Maya Patel: End of recording.

Notes on transcript: occasional ASR errors present (e.g., "reclef" instead of "relic?" or "reclaf"), speaker attributions auto-detected in places. Some timestamps approximate sampling points.
